data_points.claim: The 4ths-and-5ths layout is the only standardised note layout in the entire steelband family.

Anthony 'Muffman' Williams laid out the 'spider web' tenor pan in a cycle of fourths and fifths; sources date it to 1953, after an extended study using sketches and calculations because he believed note placement was why some notes had inferior tone.

On a piano each note has its own string and hammer and sounds independently; on a steelpan every note lives on the same sheet of steel, so notes that are dissonant are placed physically far apart to stop them interfering.
data_points.source_name: Jace Daniel - Steel Drum Tuning & Layout

data_points.claim: Notes a fourth, fifth, or octave apart reinforce a struck note's harmonic spectrum, so the layout puts those neighbours under the hand; semitone neighbours are pushed to opposite sides of the drum.

common_questions: Why aren't the notes in order?
How does anyone learn to play that?
Who decided where the notes go?

misconceptions.myth: A steelpan is laid out low-to-high like a piano keyboard.
misconceptions.reality: The tenor pan is arranged in a cycle of fourths and fifths; adjacent notes are a fourth or a fifth apart, not a semitone.

misconceptions.myth: The 'spider web' pattern is just decorative.
misconceptions.reality: It is acoustic engineering: harmonically related notes sit together to reinforce tone; dissonant notes are exiled to opposite sides so they don't interfere through the shared steel.

audience_insights.knowledge_level: General audience knows a steelpan by sound, not by construction. Assumes pitch-order layout. No music-theory needed for the payoff; the reveal is visual.
pain_points: Keyboard players find the pan disorienting because none of their spatial intuition transfers.

angles_discovered.name: This isn't a piano
angles_discovered.hook: You think you know how a steelpan works. Look where the notes actually are.
angles_discovered.why_now: Evergreen; the assumption it breaks is near-universal and the reveal is purely visual.

angles_discovered.name: One sheet of steel
angles_discovered.hook: Every note on a steelpan is stuck to every other note. That's why the layout looks insane.
angles_discovered.why_now: The physical payoff turns 'weird' into 'genius' - strongest completion driver.

angles_discovered.name: The man who drew the map
angles_discovered.hook: In 1953 one man sketched where every note should go. The whole world still uses his drawing.
angles_discovered.why_now: Human story plus a scale payoff; ties the layout to a named Trinidadian pioneer.
